zone: Mount Saul — Indian Creek and Airplane Lake, White River
_areas_note: One peak, its own file, because Mount Saul shares the White River road with the Glacier Peak zone and shares no trail with it. From the White River trailhead at the road end above Lake Wenatchee, four trails leave in different directions, and which one you take decides the trip entirely. Mount Saul, 7,293 ft, is an INDIAN CREEK peak: the Indian Creek trail runs southwest up its own valley toward Indian Pass, and about four and a half miles along it an unsigned climbers' path turns off and climbs some two thousand two hundred feet to Airplane Lake in the depression under the peak's upper east slopes. NOT DUPLICATED from the Glacier Peak and DaKobed file, which covers the OTHER trail up this same road: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin are reached by the White River trail and the Boulder Creek trail, heading north and east up the valley for Clark Mountain and Tenpeak, and a party sent there for Saul has been sent up a different drainage for a different mountain. Nothing below repeats those camps, and the roadhead entry here covers the drive-in campgrounds on the White River road, which that file describes only in passing and does not list as sites. The peak has a bare granite top and a sheer northwest face, and the standard line comes at it from the east side above the lake — so the lake is the camp and there is no sensible alternative. LOWER INDIAN CREEK IS BURN. A fire came through this drainage in 2016 and the trail passes through the scar; expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. ACCESS IN 2026 HAS BEEN CLOSED TWICE OVER. The White River road, road 6400, is named in the storm-damage road order following the December 2025 floods, effective from May 2026 and written to run into 2027, and it also sits inside the large fire closure that took effect across the Wenatchee River and Entiat districts in early August 2026 and ran to the end of October, shutting over sixty trails in the two districts. Confirm the road and the Indian Creek trail are open before planning around any of this.

sites.name: Airplane Lake
sites.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.
sites.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
sites.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.

sites.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
sites.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.
sites.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
sites.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.

sites.name: White River road end trailhead
sites.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.
sites.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
sites.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART AND HAS BEEN CLOSED TWICE IN ONE SEASON. It is named in the storm-damage closure order following the December 2025 floods, which runs into 2027 with no reopening estimate, and it sat inside the summer 2026 fire closure across the Wenatchee River and Entiat districts as well. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.

sites.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
sites.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.
sites.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
sites.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.
